issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. Being alone with women is not a plausible primary trigger for partner violence in a female patient unless there is additional trauma history not represented elsewhere, and military/police uniforms also suggest a different threat context that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: The memory/appraisal pattern centers on guilt and global identity damage, but the selected triggers point toward external threat cues unrelated to intimate-partner violence. This creates a cross-node mismatch: the triggers imply one trauma context, while memory and appraisals imply another.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is not impossible, but in this profile it intensifies the mismatch because the appraisals are extremely global and identity-based while the trigger content is narrow and externally themed in ways not linked to the romantic-partner abuse formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: Military or police uniforms are not impossible as triggers after intimate partner physical abuse, but in this profile they are hard to justify because no other trigger, memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy item links the trauma to police/military involvement, authority figures, or uniformed responders. This makes the trigger feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
issues.explanation: This item is not impossible, but alongside the more specific interpersonal/self-related profile (self-blame, guilt on recall, being alone with men, body-focused avoidance, belonging nowhere), a global 'completely destroyed' worldview reads broader than the rest of the node and may overstate the appraisal pattern relative to the otherwise relationship- and self-focused presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reflects fear, hypervigilance, avoidance, mistrust, and tension after intimate partner physical abuse. It pulls toward a more disinhibited presentation that is not supported by the trigger, memory, appraisal, or other strategy items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Own Body' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The selected triggers, memories, threats, and appraisals center on interpersonal danger, guilt, and mistrust rather than body-focused trauma responses. This item is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the main formulation compared with the other avoidance item.

vignette:
Aroha is a twenty-year-old Māori woman who works as an interior designer and recently married the man who would go on to abuse her. The relationship deteriorated quickly after the wedding. Over several months, her husband's rages escalated from verbal humiliation to physical violence - he would grab her by the throat in the kitchen, slam her against walls in darkened hallways, and scream at a volume that left her ears ringing long after the room fell silent. The last incident occurred when she was alone in their apartment at night; he cornered her in an unlit room, and the combination of the darkness, his proximity, and the explosive sound of his voice fused into a single overwhelming experience. It is this constellation of details - loud sounds, enclosed spaces without light, the presence of men in close quarters - that now reaches forward into her daily life with a force she struggles to contain.

Aroha sought help approximately three months after leaving the relationship, presenting with a PCL-5 score of 37. She works in a field that requires her to visit construction sites and meet with contractors, the majority of whom are men. On a recent site visit, a nail gun fired nearby and she felt her body lock - heart hammering, jaw clenching, every muscle braced as though impact were seconds away. That state of physical readiness does not fully subside between episodes; she describes her body as permanently tensed, and she scans constantly, checking over her shoulder in corridors and car parks, unable to shake the conviction that someone is behind her. When a trigger fires - a raised male voice in an adjacent office, a moment of being alone with a male colleague to review plans - the threat response ignites immediately, and she finds herself engineering reasons to leave the room, rescheduling meetings, and choosing routes through the building that keep her near other women. She has begun avoiding any circumstance that carries even a faint resemblance to the abuse: she will not enter a room with the lights off, refuses to remain alone in a building after hours, and has declined several evening client consultations that would have advanced her career.

These avoidance patterns have quietly narrowed her world, and the narrowing itself has become evidence for a belief she cannot shake - that her life has been destroyed, that she no longer belongs anywhere, that people cannot be trusted. When she avoids a colleague or declines a meeting, she is left alone with her thoughts, and the isolation confirms rather than relieves her sense of permanent displacement. The avoidance also means she never stays long enough in a triggering situation to learn that danger does not follow, so the situations themselves retain their charge; the mere anticipation of encountering a loud noise or being alone with a man is enough to reactivate the body-level alarm she is trying to escape.

Her memories of the abuse are not orderly. When she tries to describe what happened - to herself, to the one friend she has partially confided in - she loses the thread, the account fragmenting before she can reach its end. More disturbing to her are the moments when the full emotional weight of the abuse arrives without any accompanying image: a wave of terror and shame that seems sourceless, which she finds more frightening than the flashbacks themselves because she cannot locate what triggered it. When she does recall the events clearly, the dominant feeling is not fear but guilt - she returns compulsively to the question of what she did to provoke him, replaying her own words and choices in the weeks before each incident. This self-blame loops back into her negative appraisals: if she caused it, then she is the kind of person who invites harm, which means she belongs nowhere safe. These appraisals in turn keep the threat system elevated; believing she is permanently damaged and untrustworthy of protection, she remains vigilant as though danger is her natural condition. The memories themselves can act as triggers - a recalled fragment of his voice or the sensation of darkness is enough to send her body back onto alert, which then drives her further into avoidance and deeper into the belief that ordinary life is no longer available to her.

What finally brought Aroha to seek help was a morning when she sat in her car outside a client's office for forty minutes, unable to go in because a male contractor's van was parked outside. She missed the appointment entirely. She told the intake clinician that she was most afraid she would never trust anyone again - and most hoping, quietly, that she was wrong.
